tldr: By decoupling global navigation and approach from local dexterous grasping in large-scale simulation and distilling them into a single policy that coordinates the base, arm, hand, and active camera directly from point clouds, COWBOY achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer that adapts whole-body motion to object and scene geometry in complex, unseen real-world environments.
hero_caption: A single vision policy learned by COWBOY autonomously adapts its base placement, approach direction, and grasp posture based on object geometry and surrounding obstacles across diverse real-world scenes not directly modeled in simulation—such as inside shelves, on sofas, cluttered tables, and drawers.
overview:
When humans pick up an object, they naturally change where they stand, where they look, and how they reach depending on whether the item is on an open desk, deep inside a narrow shelf, or in a drawer. In contrast, conventional robot reinforcement learning (RL) has mostly focused on object shape generalization in single environments like a fixed tabletop. Adapting the mobile base, arm, hand, and gaze altogether to the "spatial context"—such as obstacle layouts and visual occlusions—has been extremely difficult. Training 32 degrees of freedom (DoF) end-to-end with RL directly from high-dimensional point clouds causes reward engineering to break down, preventing learning from progressing.

To tackle this, the authors propose "COWBOY," a framework that decouples the problem into two stages: a "global whole-body approach" that moves the end-effector near the target while avoiding obstacles, and "local grasping manipulation" involving contact near the hand. Global reaching is handled by a fast whole-body controller (WBC) running across thousands of parallel scenes on a GPU, while local manipulation is trained as three prototypical grasping RL experts. The combined teacher behaviors are then distilled via DAgger (imitation learning) into a single Transformer vision policy that takes point clouds from a base LiDAR and an actuated RGB-D camera as input.

In evaluations across more than 8,000 unseen simulation scenes and 24 diverse, cluttered real-world environments (such as offices and cafeterias) with over 100 unseen objects, the method achieved a remarkable 91% grasp success rate zero-shot, without any real-world fine-tuning. Even for the very same object, the robot slides its hand in from the side if it is on a shelf, grasps from above on a table, and extends its arm to compensate when the base is blocked by obstacles—demonstrating true "contextual whole-body manipulation."
contributions: Built an obstacle-avoiding, active-vision-integrated whole-body controller (WBC) based on Geometric Fabrics, capable of parallel computation across 4,096 environments on a GPU (0.03 ms per environment).

Proposed a training paradigm that decouples whole-body manipulation into "global reaching via WBC" and "local RL experts," generating scalable teacher data by reusing just three local policies across thousands of diverse full-scene layouts.
Developed a fast parallel point cloud and LiDAR renderer to distill the teacher's whole-body coordination into a single vision policy that directly drives 32 DoF from partially observed point clouds.

Demonstrated contextual adaptation without prior instructions across 24 real-world scenes and 100 unseen objects (including novel furniture and household items), achieving a 91% zero-shot grasping success rate.

sections.heading: Why do mobile robots struggle to "read the room" with whole-body motion?
sections.summary: Mobile manipulators operating in the real world must adapt their whole-body coordination not just to object shapes, but also to where objects are placed. However, end-to-end RL controlling the base, arm, hand, and camera from high-dimensional point clouds has historically been infeasible due to exploration and reward design bottlenecks. COWBOY overcomes this challenge, enabling a whole-body manipulation policy that transfers zero-shot from thousands of simulated scenes to the real world.
sections.details:
In daily life, when picking up a mug, humans easily reach forward from the front if it is on an open table, but duck and reach around obstacles if it is deep inside a drawer or shelf. This ability to instantly decide "where to stand, where to look, and how to reach" based on surrounding geometric context is what this paper calls "Contextual Whole-Body Manipulation."

Simulation-based reinforcement learning (Sim-to-Real RL) is a promising approach for gathering diverse data safely and at scale. However, recent works have mostly remained limited to "object shape generalization" on a single tabletop, falling short of "scene layout generalization." Forcing a high-DoF robot to learn high-level geometric decisions—such as obstacle avoidance, blind spots, and the trade-off between base placement and arm reachability—directly through end-to-end RL causes the state space to explode and reward design to collapse.

COWBOY (Contextual Whole-Body Manipulation Framework) elegantly overcomes this hurdle. The key idea is a complete decoupling of "global reaching in free space" and "contact-rich local manipulation." The former is delegated to a GPU-parallel geometric whole-body controller (WBC) that can solve thousands of scenes simultaneously, while only the latter is learned via RL in a compact local volume. By distilling the combined teacher policy into a single student policy that takes partial point clouds from onboard sensors, the authors obtain a whole-body control policy that operates zero-shot in high-dimensional, partially observed real-world environments.

sections.heading: At the intersection of whole-body control, sim-to-real, and reactive control
sections.summary: Imitation learning from real-world demonstrations suffers from high data-collection costs, while prior whole-body RL has been confined to low-constraint settings. Furthermore, existing optimization-based whole-body controllers are ill-suited for parallel computation. COWBOY overcomes the parallel scaling barrier by pairing GPU-friendly Geometric Fabrics with local RL.
sections.details:
To understand the positioning of this work, let us review three relevant research trends.

### Mobile Manipulation and Whole-Body Control
While imitation learning from teleoperation or human demonstrations has shown impressive results, it requires collecting new trajectory data whenever the environment changes—re-learning where to park the base and which direction to reach from. This imposes severe limits on real-world scalability. On the other hand, end-to-end whole-body control via simulation RL has also been actively explored, but most works remain restricted to flat obstacle-free grounds or simple door/drawer opening tasks with limited environmental variation.

### Sim-to-Real for Manipulation
Dexterous in-hand manipulation and grasping have achieved remarkable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Recently, policies taking point clouds or depth inputs have emerged, yet the vast majority operate on fixed-base arms. Some studies combine local policies with global planners (such as ManipGen), but relying on planners that assume complete environment models at inference time makes them brittle in noisy, occluded real-world mobile robot scenarios.

### Implementation Trade-offs in Whole-Body Controllers (WBC)
Quadratic Programming (QP) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) are widely used to coordinate redundant arm and base degrees of freedom while simultaneously handling gaze control and collision avoidance. However, because they solve constrained optimizations online for each environment, their computational cost is far too heavy for batched parallel simulation of thousands of environments in RL. Therefore, this work focuses on "Geometric Fabrics," which can reactively synthesize multiple tasks as tensor products over a fixed computational graph.

The right diagram illustrates the role of the parallel WBC based on Geometric Fabrics, which concurrently computes end-effector reaching, gaze tracking, and collision avoidance on the GPU.

sections.heading: COWBOY's approach: Decouple, reuse, and distill global approach and local RL
sections.summary: COWBOY pairs a GPU-parallel Geometric Fabrics WBC for global approach with contact-rich grasping RL experts trained in local bounding boxes. By embedding just three local experts across thousands of cluttered full scenes as teachers, the framework distills their behaviors via DAgger into a single Transformer policy driven by onboard LiDAR and active camera point clouds.
sections.details:
COWBOY's overall architecture features a clever three-stage structure designed to maximize scalability.

### 3.1 Vectorized Environment-Aware WBC
First, the authors build a whole-body controller that operates across thousands of simulation environments simultaneously. They adopt Geometric Fabrics, which defines motion objectives—such as end-effector reaching and obstacle repulsion—as geometric "forces" and "metric weight matrices" in task space, pulling them back into joint space to combine them. This approach integrates seamlessly with GPU tensor parallelism, processing 4,096 environments in Isaac Gym at a blistering speed of effectively 0.03 ms per step.

The controller introduces a "Base Attractor (BA)" that automatically drives the base to an appropriate distance based on the target position, and an "End-Effector Attractor (EEA)" that prioritizes precise arm reaching once the base is close. This naturally produces a coarse-to-fine coordinated motion: "the base drives when far, and the arm extends when near." Furthermore, obstacle repulsion terms approximating robot bodies with spheres and an active gaze control term that keeps the camera locked on the object are combined simultaneously.

### 3.2 Local Reinforcement Learning Experts
Next, RL is used to learn "contact manipulation" once the end-effector reaches the vicinity of the object. The crucial insight is to train the RL not on the full scene, but strictly within a local bounding box (local frame) extending several tens of centimeters around the object. Defining relative observations and actions in the end-effector frame, three experts were trained using PPO according to surrounding obstacle wall layouts:
- **Top-down grasp**: For environments with open space above, such as open boxes or drawers.
- **Side-grasp**: For tall, vertical objects like bottles in unobstructed spaces.
- **Constrained side-grasp**: For environments where overhead space is also blocked, such as shelves, requiring the robot to enter from the side and pull out horizontally.

### 3.3 Full-Scene Embedding and Multi-Teacher Distillation
This is the framework's greatest strength. Because the trained local experts operate in the end-effector frame, they can be reused directly inside any massive obstacle or table layout as long as the local geometric conditions are satisfied. Local experts were embedded into thousands of randomly generated full-scene environments, forming a "teacher policy" where the WBC handles long-range approach and the local RL takes over once close.

The behavior of this composite teacher is then distilled into a single point-cloud-based student Transformer policy using DAgger (Dataset Aggregation). The student takes only partial point clouds from the base 3D LiDAR and the actuated pan-tilt RGB-D camera, along with robot proprioception, and directly outputs commands across all 32 DoF (base velocity, arm, hand, and neck). This produces a deployable real-world policy free of any privileged simulation states.

captions.F3: Conceptual diagram of local RL policies and full-scene rollout. The same grasping policy trained in a local bounding box (red outline) is embedded into completely different full scenes—such as drawers, cluttered desks, and cardboard boxes—and connected with the WBC's global approach to generate countless teacher trajectories.
captions.F8: Visualization of the three trained local RL experts. From left to right: "Top-down", "Side Grasp", and "Constrained Side Grasp," efficiently acquiring contact behaviors tailored to surrounding wall constraints.

sections.heading: Venturing into the unknown: Stress-testing across 24 real scenes and 100 objects
sections.summary: Grasping experiments were conducted using a real Franka arm, LEAP Hand, mobile base, and actuated camera across 24 in-the-wild real-world scenes and 100 unseen objects not present in simulation. Initializing the 3D target position via SAM3 and autoregressively tracking it with an auxiliary head, the study evaluated generalization and ablations on both fixed and random object sets.
sections.details:
The physical robot comprises an omnidirectional mobile base (TidyBot++), a 7-DoF Franka arm, a 16-DoF dexterous multi-finger hand (LEAP Hand), an active camera neck (ARX X5 arm + RealSense D435), and a base-mounted 3D LiDAR (Unitree L2), providing 32 DoF in total.

### Real-Robot Experimental Setup
The evaluation featured "24 in-the-wild real scenes" drawn from labs, office lounges, cafeterias, and more. These were completely independent of the simulation procedural generation rules and included office chairs, refrigerators, stair landings, and counters of varying heights. Evaluation objects consisted of diverse daily items never seen during simulation training (plush toys, detergent bottles, tools, fruits, etc.). Testing evaluated both a "fixed set of 20 objects" tested across all scenes and a "random set of 5 objects drawn from 100 objects" per scene, each tested under three initial poses. A trial was marked successful if the object was lifted at least 10 cm without colliding with obstacles.

### Real-World Perception Pipeline
To specify "which object to pick" in a cluttered scene, the system uses SAM3, a promptable segmentation model. The 3D point cloud centroid computed from the mask in the initial frame serves as the initial target position. Afterward, an auxiliary prediction head within the student network autoregressively tracks it at 60 Hz. SAM3 runs in the background at 3 Hz to periodically correct tracking drift.

### Simulation Evaluation and Ablations
Using 8,192 unseen simulation scenes and 150 objects, COWBOY was benchmarked against baselines (end-to-end RL and ManipGen). Rigorous ablation studies were also conducted, stripping away components such as "fixing the active camera," "removing the LiDAR," "providing ground-truth point clouds without sensor rendering," and "replacing the WBC with basic inverse kinematics (IK)."

captions.F6: The collection of unseen evaluation objects used in real-robot experiments. The left shows 100 random objects used to evaluate generalization, while the right displays the fixed set of 20 objects used to evaluate contextual adaptation across all scenes. Many irregular and deformable objects are included.

sections.heading: 91% real-world success! Autonomously adapting both "where to stand" and "how to grasp"
sections.summary: COWBOY achieved a 91% average zero-shot success rate across 24 real-world environments, dramatically outperforming end-to-end RL (0%) and ManipGen (63.8%). The robot demonstrated sophisticated contextual adaptation by autonomously adjusting its approach direction and base parking spot based on obstacle geometry, while ablations confirmed the indispensability of active vision and LiDAR point clouds.
sections.details:
Here are the key takeaways from the experimental results, organized around the paper's core questions:

### Remarkable Zero-Shot Transfer to Unseen Scenes and Objects
The average grasping success rate across the 24 real-world scenes reached **91%**. High success was maintained even in narrow spaces unmodeled in simulation, such as inside refrigerators or beside staircases. The only slight drop occurred in constrained shelf settings requiring a horizontal reach, where success fell to the low 80% range—primarily due to the inherent risk of tipping objects over during side approaches—demonstrating strong overall robustness.

### Emergence of Contextual Whole-Body Control
Remarkably, without any external instructions specifying "grasp from above," "grasp from the side," or "stop the base here," the policy autonomously adapted its whole-body motion based purely on point cloud geometry. For instance, in the same sofa scene, it approached a tall bottle from the side while descending from above for a flat plush toy. When obstacles like stools blocked the base, it halted early and reached forward with its arm, showing clear whole-body coordination.

### Comparison with Baselines (Simulation)
In 8,000 unseen simulation scenes, end-to-end RL from point clouds suffered a **0% success rate** (despite achieving 96% in obstacle-free open space, proving that learning collision avoidance and grasping simultaneously causes RL to fail). Meanwhile, ManipGen, which combines VLMs with motion planning, achieved an average of 63.8%. Because ManipGen plans intermediate waypoints separately, it frequently ran into arm singularities. In contrast, COWBOY directly outputs actions from approach to manipulation via a single policy, achieving an 87.9% success rate in simulation.

### Key Insights from Ablation Studies
- **Active Vision**: Fixing the camera neck facing forward caused the robot to lose sight of objects near the floor or inside boxes, resulting in a severe drop in success.
- **Base LiDAR**: Because the wrist/head cameras have narrow fields of view with blind spots directly in front of the base, removing LiDAR caused frequent collisions between the base and table legs or shelf sides.
- **Partial-Observation Simulation**: A model trained on ground-truth full point clouds scored high in simulation but failed completely on the real robot due to real-world occlusions.
- **WBC Formulation**: Using naive weighted IK as a teacher caused the arm to overextend and hit joint limits or singularities instead of driving the base, severely degrading teacher trajectory quality.

captions.F5: Overview of grasping success rates across 24 real-world scenes. Evaluated across diverse environments including homes, offices, and kitchens, COWBOY achieved a high average success rate of 91% over 25 objects × 3 trials per scene.

sections.heading: New horizons for whole-body manipulation and the path to functional grasping
sections.summary: By uniting a GPU-parallel WBC with local RL experts, COWBOY establishes a scalable framework for learning whole-body manipulation from simulation to reality. Looking ahead, explicitly specifying task-dependent grasp modes and expanding to longer-horizon tasks remain key challenges.
sections.details:
This paper addresses the central hurdle preventing mobile manipulators from thriving in unstructured environments: whole-body adaptation to spatial context. Decoupling global approach into a geometric WBC and local contact into RL experts, then distilling both into a single vision Transformer, provides a powerful paradigm for building future robot foundation models.

### Limitations and Future Directions
While COWBOY excels at inferring natural grasping strategies from surrounding geometry, it does not yet support "functional grasping"—where the grasp location on the same mug should vary depending on whether the downstream task is to hand it to a person or drink from it. Future work will need to condition the policy on downstream task intent via language prompts or other signals.

Nonetheless, placing a robot in an unfamiliar room with novel furniture and watching it autonomously find a collision-free path to dexterously retrieve items represents a major step toward general-purpose assistant robots.

sections.heading: Appendix: Behind the scenes of parallel WBC and fast sensor rendering
sections.summary: This section details the mathematical formulation of the Geometric Fabrics WBC and the custom vectorized point-cloud and LiDAR simulator capable of processing 1,024 environments in 0.25 seconds. These technical foundations underpin COWBOY's large-scale distillation.
sections.details:
The massive scale of COWBOY's training is made possible by thorough GPU parallelization techniques detailed in the appendix.

### Why Geometric Fabrics?
Standard optimization-based WBCs (such as QP or MPC) change their active inequality constraint sets (e.g., collision avoidance) per environment, making them poorly suited for GPU SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) parallelism. In contrast, Geometric Fabrics pulls task-space equations of motion back into joint space ($J^T M J$) using differential geometry. Because this relies purely on batched matrix multiplications and reductions, collision avoidance and gaze tracking across 4,096 environments can be evaluated in one go on the GPU as a fixed computational graph without branching.

### Vectorized Sensor Simulator Engineering
Distilling the student policy requires point cloud data from thousands of environments, but rendering camera images and LiDAR scans via conventional graphics pipelines for thousands of robots is impossible due to GPU memory and throughput limits. To overcome this, the authors implemented camera projection, z-buffer occlusion culling, and LiDAR hemisphere ray casting entirely as custom PyTorch tensor operations over pre-sampled scene surface meshes. On a single A6000 GPU, this renders depth images for 1,024 environments in 0.07 seconds and LiDAR point clouds in 0.25 seconds, enabling 8,192-parallel distillation across 8 GPUs.

takeaways: Decoupling global navigation/approach (WBC) from local contact manipulation (RL) prevents exploration space explosion while scaling effortlessly to thousands of diverse scenes.
Because Geometric Fabrics can be formulated as a fixed computational graph, it is exceptionally well-suited as a collision-avoiding whole-body controller for large-scale parallel simulation.
Real-world mobile manipulation critically relies on a complementary sensor suite: active vision to track the target and hand, paired with base LiDAR to monitor blind spots and foot-level obstacles.
Sim-to-real transfer will fail unless simulation faithfully renders partial observations (occlusions and sensor field-of-view limits) rather than feeding privileged ground-truth point clouds.
limitations: The system does not support functional grasping conditioned on downstream task intent (e.g., how the object will be used after pickup), picking a near-unique grasp determined primarily by geometry and environmental constraints.
In tight spaces like deep shelves that enforce a horizontal approach, the failure rate remains relatively high due to the hand accidentally knocking objects over upon contact.
Initial target identification relies on an external vision model (SAM3), leaving room for improvement in autonomous error recovery if the initial detection fails.
